title: Renovation Project Gallery | Genstone Construction
metaDescription: Featured Genstone renovations in Tampa, Barrington and Woodridge, with notes on the finish choices and what investors can take from each project.
lede: Explore real projects that show the quality, craftsmanship and attention to detail behind a Genstone Construction renovation. Alongside each one, we've added notes on the decisions behind the finishes and what an investor planning a similar project can take from it, whether the goal is a resale, a rental or a refinance.

sections.body:
Photos show the finished result. They don't show the choices that produced it: which rooms got the budget, which original features were kept, and which finishes were picked because they photograph well versus because they hold up. For an investor, those choices are the useful part.

The three projects below cover a whole-home renovation in Florida and two Chicago-area remodels focused on the rooms that carry the most weight with buyers and renters: kitchens, baths and the main living space. As you look through them, notice how much of the impact comes from a small number of well-placed decisions, and how consistent each house is from room to room.

This whole-home renovation refreshed every corner of a classic bungalow while preserving its timeless charm. Wide-plank hardwood floors, soft blue walls and crisp crown molding carry through bright, open living spaces. The kitchen is the showpiece, with white shaker cabinets and glass-front uppers, brushed gold hardware and fixtures, a marble mosaic backsplash with a pot filler, and a waterfall island topped with elegant marble-look countertops. Updated stairs, a stylish powder room and a restored front porch complete a home that feels fresh, welcoming and move-in ready.

What an investor can take from it: on an older bungalow, the character is part of the value. Crown molding, a restored porch and wood floors tell buyers the house was renovated with care rather than stripped and flipped. The budget is concentrated where buyers spend their time on a tour, in the kitchen, while the rest of the house is tied together with one floor and one wall color. The marble-look countertops deliver the look of stone with a material that's easier to live with. And a restored front porch is the first thing a buyer sees, in person and in the listing photos.

This multi-room renovation brought fresh style and function to the fireplace, the kitchen and the bathroom. In the living room, a floor-to-ceiling rock tile fireplace surround with a raised stone hearth creates a striking focal point. The kitchen features crisp white shaker cabinets, granite countertops, a white subway tile backsplash, and matte black hardware and lighting. The bathroom pairs a natural wood vanity and marble-look top with matte black fixtures and a wood-look tile accent wall in the tub surround for a warm, modern finish.

What an investor can take from it: not every property needs a whole-home renovation. Three targeted rooms changed how this house reads. The fireplace surround turns an existing feature into the focal point of the living room. The kitchen uses classic, widely available materials (shaker cabinets, granite, subway tile) and gets its personality from the matte black hardware and lighting, which are inexpensive to change later. Repeating matte black in the bath ties the rooms together. The wood-look tile in the tub surround adds warmth in a wet area where real wood wouldn't hold up.

This kitchen remodel pairs classic style with everyday function. Walnut-stained maple shaker cabinets bring warmth and generous storage, while a large center island adds prep space and a natural gathering spot. A white subway tile backsplash, veined countertops, stainless steel appliances and new recessed lighting complete a bright, inviting space that flows easily into the adjoining dining area.

What an investor can take from it: a single well-planned kitchen can carry a property. Stained wood cabinets are a deliberate change from all-white kitchens and help a listing stand apart, while the subway tile and veined countertops keep the room broadly appealing. The island adds storage and work surface buyers and tenants both value. Recessed lighting is a small line item that changes how the room looks in person and in photos. Stainless appliances remain what most buyers expect to see in a renovated kitchen.

A few patterns run through every project here, and they apply to most investor renovations.

- The kitchen gets the most attention. In all three homes it carries the largest share of the visual impact.
- Finishes stay consistent. One floor, one hardware finish and one paint palette make a house feel finished and keep material ordering simpler.
- Classic base, current accents. Shaker cabinets and subway tile are timeless and easy to match later. Hardware, lighting and fixtures carry the current style and can be updated cheaply.
- Lighting is part of the scope. New fixtures and recessed lighting help in showings and in listing photos.
- Existing features are used, not ignored. A fireplace or a porch can become a selling point for far less than adding something new.

When Genstone writes a scope, these are the kinds of trade-offs we lay out, matched to your ARV and your strategy.
